segments.title: A personal visit to Enkoji Temple
segments.body: An earlier attempt by the tour group went to the wrong place, so this visit is made alone. It is described as a personal pilgrimage within the larger ShipShape naval-history tour of Japan. Enkoji, described as a small temple in a small Japanese city, is the place where Mitsumasa Yonai is remembered. The account begins with the destination and the reason for leaving the group, then turns to Yonai’s historical reputation.

evidence.note: Travelling alone to Enkoji Temple to see the place where Yonai is remembered.

segments.summary: The search for Enkoji Temple becomes a personal pilgrimage to the place where Mitsumasa Yonai is remembered.

segments.title: Yonai as an overlooked Japanese leader
segments.body: Admiral Henderson was the Royal Navy’s Third Sea Lord before the Second World War. His example provides a parallel for Yonai: both are presented as important senior naval figures who were overshadowed by louder personalities. Yonai remains important to Japan’s story, yet he receives less attention in Western recollections of the war. The difficulty of reaching his memorial adds meaning to the journey, especially since Henderson has no comparable memorial. The visit is placed alongside the tour’s attention to Pearl Harbor and Yamato, explaining why Yonai is worth seeking out and remembering.

evidence.note: Interest in Yonai explained through a comparison with Admiral Henderson and more familiar Second World War subjects.

segments.summary: The comparison with Admiral Henderson presents Yonai as another senior naval figure overshadowed by louder personalities and overlooked in Western accounts of the Second World War.
